lesson.title: One Variable at a Time: Building the Primary Equation
lesson.summary: The primary equation is what you get after substituting the constraint equation into the objective function, a single variable function that ordinary derivative tools can finally be applied to directly.
lesson.body:
The primary equation is what results from substituting the constraint equation into the objective function: a single variable function that the ordinary derivative toolkit, critical numbers, the First and Second Derivative Tests, can finally be applied to directly. This substitution step is the hinge of the entire optimization method. Every tool built in local extrema analysis and concavity analysis was designed for functions of one variable. The objective function usually starts out with two, so it is not yet usable on its own. Using the constraint to eliminate one variable is what collapses the objective function into something differentiable.

Work through a full derivation with a fresh example that later chapters will finish solving. An open top box has a square base of side x and height h, and its volume must equal 32 cubic units. The objective function, the surface area to be minimized (one square base plus four rectangular sides, with no top), is S = x^2 + 4xh. The constraint equation, the fixed volume, is x^2 h = 32. Solving the constraint for h gives h = 32 / x^2.

Substitute that expression for h directly into the objective function: S(x) = x^2 + 4x(32 / x^2). Simplifying the second term, 4x times 32 over x^2 equals 128x over x^2, which reduces to 128 / x. So the primary equation is S(x) = x^2 + 128 / x, a function of x alone.

The domain has to be restated in terms of this single remaining variable too. Since x is a physical side length, x must be positive, so the domain is x > 0. Notice that once x is positive, h = 32 / x^2 automatically comes out positive as well, so no separate restriction on h is needed. Getting the domain right matters just as much as the algebra, since reasoning about a global minimum later depends on knowing exactly which values of x are physically allowed.

With S(x) = x^2 + 128 / x in hand, the box problem is finally in a form that can be differentiated exactly like any function from local extrema analysis. Actually finding the optimal dimensions, taking the derivative, solving for critical numbers, and classifying them, is where the process gets formalized end to end in the next chapter.
